stem: Developer A's Claude Code follows the team's API naming conventions perfectly. Developer B, who joined last week, gets inconsistent naming — both work on the same repo and branch. What is the most likely root cause?

options.label: A
options.body: The naming conventions live in Developer A's user-level CLAUDE.md (~/.claude/CLAUDE.md) rather than in project-level config.
options.rationale: Correct. User-level CLAUDE.md isn't version-controlled or shared via git. A has it locally; B, who just cloned, doesn't. Moving the rules to project config (.claude/CLAUDE.md or root CLAUDE.md) fixes it.

options.label: B
options.body: Developer B simply hasn't run the /memory command yet to load the team's naming-convention configuration files onto their machine.
options.rationale: /memory is a diagnostic that shows which files are loaded — it doesn't trigger loading. Config loads automatically from file location.

options.label: C
options.body: Developer B needs to install an MCP server before they can access the team's naming-convention rules for the API code.
options.rationale: MCP servers provide tool integrations, not CLAUDE.md configuration. Conventions are config, not tools.

options.label: D
options.body: The conventions live in a .claude/rules/ file that Developer B's particular system happens not to support on their setup.
options.rationale: .claude/rules/ files are inside the repo and version-controlled — B would receive them on clone.

stem: A monorepo has packages/api/ with API conventions and packages/frontend/ with component conventions. Each package should follow its own standards without duplicating shared conventions. What's the correct configuration?

options.label: A
options.body: Project-level CLAUDE.md with @import for shared standards, plus a directory-level CLAUDE.md in each package importing only package-specific standards.
options.rationale: Correct. @import enables modular organization — shared standards live once and are imported where needed; package-specific rules live in directory-level CLAUDE.md. No duplication.

options.label: B
options.body: Put a directory-level CLAUDE.md in each package that contains all of the conventions, including its own full copy of the shared standards, so each package is self-contained.
options.rationale: Duplicates the shared conventions in every package, creating maintenance burden and drift.

options.label: C
options.body: Put all of the conventions in user-level config and have each developer manually copy the sections relevant to whichever package they happen to be working in.
options.rationale: User-level config is personal and not shared via git — this fails for new team members.

options.label: D
options.body: Create one skill per package that developers manually invoke before they begin working inside that particular package's directory each time.
options.rationale: Skills load on-demand; conventions should apply to every edit as always-in-context guidance, which CLAUDE.md provides.

stem: A skill performs codebase analysis and floods the main conversation with file listings, dependency graphs, and code excerpts. Which SKILL.md frontmatter fixes this?

options.label: A
options.body: context: fork — run the skill in an isolated sub-agent so its verbose output stays contained and the main conversation gets only the summary.
options.rationale: Correct. context: fork isolates the skill's context; the main window stays clean for subsequent work.

options.label: B
options.body: Set allowed-tools: [Read, Grep, Glob] on the skill to limit the volume of codebase data it is able to access while performing the analysis.
options.rationale: allowed-tools governs tool access, not output volume — the skill would still produce verbose output with the permitted tools.

options.label: C
options.body: Set argument-hint: "Specify a narrow scope" so the skill is prompted to reduce how much analysis it performs on each run it does.
options.rationale: argument-hint documents expected input parameters; it doesn't control output volume.

options.label: D
options.body: Set output-limit: 1000 in the frontmatter to cap the number of tokens the skill is permitted to produce back into the conversation.
options.rationale: output-limit is not a valid SKILL.md frontmatter option — it doesn't exist.

stem: Test files are co-located with source across 50+ directories (Button.test.tsx next to Button.tsx). The team wants all tests to follow the same conventions regardless of location. Most maintainable approach?

options.label: A
options.body: A rule file in .claude/rules/ with YAML frontmatter paths: ["**/*.test.tsx", "**/*.test.ts"] containing the test conventions.
options.rationale: Correct. Glob patterns match test files across the whole codebase and load automatically when editing any of them — one file covers all 50+ directories with zero maintenance.

options.label: B
options.body: Place a CLAUDE.md in every one of the 50-plus directories that contain test files, each holding its own copy of the test conventions.
options.rationale: 50+ directories means massive duplication; every change touches 50+ files and new directories need new copies. Drift is inevitable.

options.label: C
options.body: Add all of the test conventions to the root CLAUDE.md so they are loaded in every session regardless of whether test files are being edited.
options.rationale: Root CLAUDE.md loads every session — test rules would burn tokens even when editing non-test files.

options.label: D
options.body: Create a skill in .claude/skills/ that developers remember to invoke each time before they start writing a new set of test files.
options.rationale: Relies on developers remembering to invoke it. Path-specific rules load automatically when Claude reads a matching file — no human step.

stem: A developer edits src/api/auth.ts. The project has three rule files: testing.md (paths: ["**/*.test.ts"]), api-conventions.md (paths: ["src/api/**/*"]), and terraform.md (paths: ["terraform/**/*"]). Which rules load?

options.label: A
options.body: Only api-conventions.md, because the file matches src/api/**/*.
options.rationale: Correct. auth.ts matches src/api/**/*. It isn't a *.test.ts file and isn't under terraform/, so those rules don't load.

options.label: B
options.body: All three, because they're all in .claude/rules/.
options.rationale: Being in .claude/rules/ doesn't mean automatic loading — rules load only when the edited file matches their glob.

options.label: C
options.body: api-conventions.md and testing.md, because the file is in src/.
options.rationale: testing.md needs a *.test.ts file; auth.ts isn't a test file, so testing rules don't load.

options.label: D
options.body: None, because path-specific rules require explicit invocation.
options.rationale: Path-specific rules load automatically when Claude reads a matching file; no invocation needed (that's skills).

stem: Three tasks: (1) restructure a monolith into microservices, (2) fix a null-pointer in one function with a clear stack trace, (3) migrate a logging library across 30 files. Which mode for each?

options.label: A
options.body: Plan mode for (1) and (3); direct execution for (2).
options.rationale: Correct. (1) has architectural decisions with multiple valid boundaries — plan mode. (3) touches 30 files and needs a consistent migration strategy first — plan mode. (2) is a clear single-function fix — direct execution.

options.label: B
options.body: Plan mode for all three, since they all involve code changes.
options.rationale: Task 2 is a well-scoped fix with a clear stack trace — plan mode adds no value.

options.label: C
options.body: Plan mode for (1); direct execution for (2) and (3).
options.rationale: Task 3 spans 30 files with API differences; without a planned pattern you risk inconsistency and missed edge cases.

options.label: D
options.body: Direct execution for all three with comprehensive upfront instructions.
options.rationale: Task 1 needs exploration of dependencies before restructuring; upfront instructions assume a structure you haven't verified.

stem: A CI script runs `claude "Analyse this PR"` but the job hangs indefinitely — logs show Claude Code waiting for interactive input. Correct fix?

options.label: A
options.body: Add the -p (--print) flag: `claude -p "Analyse this PR"`.
options.rationale: Correct. -p/--print runs headless — it processes the prompt, prints to stdout, and exits without waiting for input. The documented CI approach.

options.label: B
options.body: Set CLAUDE_HEADLESS=true before running.
options.rationale: CLAUDE_HEADLESS isn't a real Claude Code environment variable.

options.label: C
options.body: Redirect stdin from /dev/null so the command can't block waiting on interactive input.
options.rationale: A generic workaround that doesn't properly address interactive mode; -p is the correct documented flag.

options.label: D
options.body: Add a --batch flag to the claude command invocation in the CI script.
options.rationale: --batch isn't a real Claude Code CLI flag.

stem: A CI pipeline must post review findings as inline PR comments at specific file/line numbers. Which flags should be used?

options.label: A
options.body: --output-format json plus --json-schema defining file, line, severity, and message fields.
options.rationale: Correct. --output-format json gives machine-readable output and --json-schema enforces the structure, so automation can post findings at exact locations.

options.label: B
options.body: Use --output-format json on its own, without pairing it with a defined schema for the file, line, and severity fields.
options.rationale: JSON without a schema isn't guaranteed to carry the specific fields (file/line/severity/message) needed for inline commenting.

options.label: C
options.body: Use the --verbose and --line-numbers flags together to produce the structured review output for the pipeline.
options.rationale: Not valid Claude Code flags for structured output.

options.label: D
options.body: Use the --format markdown and --annotate flags to generate the inline pull-request comments for the pipeline.
options.rationale: Not valid Claude Code flags.
